qt: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:
Status of living victims of Nazi crimes in connection with Directive (EU)

In my previous questions E-002079/20251 and E-003059/20252, I drew attention to the absence of an EU mechanism for living victims of crimes committed during the Second World War. However, following the Commission’s answer, Directive (EU) 2026/1472 amending Directive 2012/29/EU was adopted. The new regulations explicitly list victims of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression – as defined in the Statute of the International Criminal Court – as categories requiring special consideration and targeted, integrated support. In light of this change in the legal situation, I would like to ask: Are living EU citizens who were victims of crimes committed by Nazi Germany during World War II covered by the rights to support and protection provided for in the amended Directive 2012/29/EU for victims of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes or the crime of aggression, and if not, which specific provisions of EU law form the basis for their exclusion from the scope of those rights?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) As rightly recalled by the Honourable Member, Directive (EU) 2026/14721 strengthens the 2012 Victims’ Rights Directive2 by requiring Member States to ensure targeted and integrated support for victims of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes or the crime of aggression, as defined in the Statute of the International Criminal Court. Under the revised Directive, these victims shall also be duly considered in the context of the individual assessment. In principle, these provisions are not limited by the date on which the crime was committed. Therefore, living EU citizens who suffered such crimes during the Second World War may fall within the scope of the Victims’ Rights Directive. Member States have two years to adopt the measures necessary to comply with most provisions of the revised Directive (until 2 July 2028). That said, the Victims’ Rights Directive, as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/1472, lays down minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime. It does not in itself establish criminal liability, reopen historical proceedings, or create an explicit compensation regime for past atrocities. The practical application of these rights depends on the circumstances of the individual case.
1 Directive (EU) 2026/1472 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2026 amending Directive

2012/29/EU establishing minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA, PE/11/2026/REV/1, OJ L, 2026/1472, 30.6.2026. 2 Directive 2012/29/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2012 establishing minimum standards on the rights, support and protection of victims of crime, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2001/220/JHA, OJ L 315, 14.11.2012, pp. 57-73.
